A pedestal is a raised base or support structure that something is placed on top of — usually to hold it up, display it, and make it stand out.

Think of a statue of a famous person in a public square. The statue doesn't sit directly on the ground. Instead, it sits on a solid block of stone or marble beneath it. That block — the thing lifting the statue up and holding it in place — is the pedestal.

The key idea is elevation for the purpose of display or prominence. A pedestal doesn't just support an object; it presents it, shows it off, and says: "Look at this. This matters."
What a pedestal typically looks like

A pedestal is usually a vertical structure — taller than it is wide — with a flat top surface where the object rests. It can be made of stone, marble, wood, or metal. You'll commonly see pedestals in:

  • Museums (holding sculptures or ancient artifacts)
  • Public parks and squares (beneath statues)
  • Art galleries (displaying busts or artwork)
  • Homes (as decorative stands for vases, plants, or figurines)

One important quality: a pedestal is not just any base. It specifically lifts something up to a visible, prominent height — making the object feel important, worthy of attention, even grand.
The figurative meaning (extremely common in everyday language)

This is where "pedestal" becomes truly powerful in English, and you'll encounter it very often.

When we say someone has been "put on a pedestal," we mean that a person is being admired or idealized to an unrealistic degree — as if they are perfect, flawless, and far above ordinary humans.

Just as a statue on a pedestal is physically elevated above the crowd and displayed as something special, a person "on a pedestal" is emotionally or mentally elevated in someone's eyes — treated as though they can do no wrong.

Example: "He put his favorite author on a pedestal and refused to hear any criticism of her work."

This figurative use almost always carries a subtle negative tone. Why? Because placing someone on a pedestal means you're not seeing them as a real, flawed human being. You're projecting an image of perfection onto them. And that's usually seen as unhealthy — both for the relationship and for your own perception of reality.

Some more examples of how this plays out:

  • A person who is deeply in love might put their partner on a pedestal, ignoring their flaws entirely — only to feel deeply disappointed later when reality sets in.
  • A fan might put a celebrity on a pedestal, treating their every word as wisdom.
  • Someone might put a parent or mentor on a pedestal, unable to accept that they could ever make a mistake.

The opposite idea is also commonly expressed: "He fell off his pedestal" — meaning someone who was once idealized and admired has now been revealed to be flawed, disappointing, or dishonest. The image of perfection has been shattered.
The single thread connecting both meanings

Whether literal or figurative, the word "pedestal" always carries the same underlying idea:

Something (or someone) is being raised up above the ordinary level — given a position of special prominence, display, or honor.

In the physical sense, that's a block of stone holding up a statue.
In the emotional or social sense, that's the act of treating someone as though they are superior, untouchable, or perfect.

• "The bronze statue stood on a marble pedestal in the center of the town square."
  • "She finally realized she had put her boss on a pedestal and expected too much from him."
  • "The pedestal in the museum displayed an ancient Roman bust."
  • "Don't put anyone on a pedestal — everyone has flaws."
  • "When the scandal broke, the politician fell from his pedestal overnight."

If you ever forget the figurative meaning, just picture the literal image: a statue, high up on its stone base, looking grand and untouchable — and you'll instantly understand what it means to put a person "on a pedestal."
